proof_nl:
Let
Q(q) := product_{i=a+1}^b ((1 - q^(r+i)) / (1 - q^i)).
For the fixed j, write
E_j := { (S, lambda) in X_j : |S| is even }
and
O_j := { (S, lambda) in X_j : |S| is odd }.
Because I is finite and every element of I is a positive integer, there are only finitely many multisets lambda with |lambda| <= j; hence X_j, E_j, and O_j are finite.

First, the coefficient of q^j in Q(q) is exactly |E_j| - |O_j|. Indeed, for each i in I,
(1 - q^(r+i)) / (1 - q^i) = (1 - q^(r+i)) * sum_{m>=0} q^(mi).
When we expand the whole product, choosing the term -q^(r+i) from the numerator factor means that i is placed into S, while choosing q^(mi) from the geometric-series factor means that lambda contains i with multiplicity m. The total exponent is then
sum_{s in S} (r+s) + |lambda|,
and the sign is (-1)^|S|. Therefore the coefficient of q^j is
sum_{(S,lambda) in X_j} (-1)^|S| = |E_j| - |O_j|.

Next, Q(q) is a polynomial. Using the cyclotomic factorization 1 - q^m = product_{d|m} Phi_d(q), the exponent of Phi_d(q) in Q(q) is
|{ i in I : d divides (r+i) }| - |{ i in I : d divides i }|.
Since I = {a+1,...,b}, this exponent is exactly
M_d(r+a,r+b) - M_d(a,b),
which is >= 0 by hypothesis. Hence every cyclotomic exponent in Q(q) is nonnegative, so Q(q) belongs to Z[q].

Now set N := r + a + b. By the standard product formula for Gaussian q-binomial coefficients,
[N choose k]_q = (q;q)_N / ((q;q)_k (q;q)_(N-k)).
Therefore
[N choose b]_q / [N choose a]_q
= ((q;q)_a (q;q)_(N-a)) / ((q;q)_b (q;q)_(N-b))
= ((q;q)_a (q;q)_(r+b)) / ((q;q)_b (q;q)_(r+a))
= Q(q),
because N-a = r+b and N-b = r+a.

We have just shown that this quotient is a polynomial. Applying the allowed Gaussian-quotient positivity statement with n = N, k = b, and l = a, it follows that every coefficient of Q(q) is nonnegative. In particular, the coefficient of q^j is nonnegative. By the first paragraph, this says
|E_j| - |O_j| >= 0,
so |E_j| >= |O_j|.

Since E_j and O_j are finite and |E_j| >= |O_j|, choose an injection f : O_j -> E_j. Define iota_j : X_j -> X_j by
- if x in O_j, set iota_j(x) := f(x);
- if x is in the image f(O_j), set iota_j(x) := f^{-1}(x);
- if x in E_j \ f(O_j), set iota_j(x) := x.
This is well-defined because f is injective, and clearly iota_j^2 = id_{X_j}; so iota_j is an involution.

If iota_j(S,lambda) = (S',lambda') != (S,lambda), then one of the two elements lies in O_j and the other lies in E_j, so |S'| and |S| have opposite parity. Equivalently,
|S'| ≡ |S| + 1 mod 2.
If iota_j(S,lambda) = (S,lambda), then (S,lambda) lies in E_j, so |S| is even.

Thus there exists an involution iota_j : X_j -> X_j with properties (1) and (2).

domain_restrictions: a and b are integers with 0 <= a <= b.
j is an integer with 0 <= j <= floor(r (b - a) / 2).
d ranges over positive integers only.
M_d counts integers m in the interval with u < m <= v that are divisible by d.
S must be a subset of I.
lambda must be a finite multiset of elements of I, with repetition allowed.
The notation |lambda| means the sum of the elements of the multiset lambda, not its cardinality.
The set X_j includes exactly those pairs (S, lambda) whose total weighted sum equals j.
The parity statement uses |S| as the cardinality of S.
An involution means a self-map whose square is the identity.
semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: Under the stated numerical and divisibility hypotheses, the set X_j admits an involution. Every non-fixed orbit pairs two elements whose subset parts have opposite parity, and every fixed point has an even-sized subset part.
quantifier_order: Fix integers a, b, r, j with 0 <= a <= b, r >= 0, and 0 <= j <= floor(r (b - a) / 2).
Define I as the integers from a + 1 through b.
For every positive integer d, define M_d(u, v) as the number of integers m such that u < m <= v and d divides m.
Assume that for every positive integer d, M_d(r + a, r + b) is at least M_d(a, b).
Define X_j to consist of all pairs (S, lambda) with S a subset of I, lambda a finite multiset of elements of I, and sum of elements of lambda plus sum over s in S of (r + s) equal to j.
There exists an involution iota_j from X_j to X_j satisfying the two parity conditions.

witness_dependencies: The existential witness iota_j depends on the fixed parameters a, b, r, and j, as well as on the universal hypothesis that M_d(r + a, r + b) >= M_d(a, b) for every positive integer d.
No additional existential witnesses are introduced besides iota_j.
For any input pair (S, lambda) in X_j, the output pair (S prime, lambda prime) is determined by iota_j; the moved-point parity condition compares the cardinalities of S and S prime.
If a pair is fixed by iota_j, the fixed-point condition requires the same S to have even cardinality.

statement_nl: Let a, b, r, j be integers with 0 <= a <= b, r >= 0, and 0 <= j <= floor(r (b - a) / 2). Put I := {a+1, a+2, ..., b}. For each positive integer d, define M_d(u,v) := |{m in Z : u < m <= v and d divides m}|, and assume M_d(r+a,r+b) >= M_d(a,b) for every positive integer d. Let X_j be the set of pairs (S, lambda) such that S is a subset of I, lambda is a finite multiset of elements of I, |lambda| denotes the sum of the elements of lambda, and |lambda| + sum_{s in S} (r + s) = j. Then there exists an involution iota_j : X_j -> X_j such that: (1) if iota_j(S,lambda) = (S',lambda') != (S,lambda), then |S'| is congruent to |S| + 1 modulo 2; and (2) if iota_j(S,lambda) = (S,lambda), then |S| is even.
